title: Apache Airflow
text:
Apache Airflow

Airflow Overview
Apache Airflow is a workflow orchestration platform used to define, schedule, and monitor data
workflows. A workflow is represented as a Directed Acyclic Graph, or DAG, where tasks describe
individual units of work and dependencies describe the order in which those tasks should run. Airflow is
commonly used in data engineering to coordinate ingestion, transformation, validation, and downstream
processing without embedding the business logic inside the scheduler itself.
DAGs, Tasks, and Dependencies
A DAG defines the structure of a workflow. Tasks may run Python functions, execute SQL, trigger
external jobs, or call other systems through operators and hooks. Dependencies such as task_a >>
task_b make the execution order explicit. This is useful for pipelines where a transformation must wait
for ingestion to finish, or a validation step must succeed before data is published. Clear dependencies
make failures easier to isolate and reruns easier to manage.
Scheduling and Reruns
Airflow can run workflows on a schedule or through manual triggers. Each scheduled run has its own
execution context, which helps teams reason about daily or hourly processing windows. Data pipelines
should still be designed to be idempotent, because orchestration tools may retry failed tasks or
operators may rerun a historical execution. A safe rerun should not create duplicate data or corrupt
previously successful output.

Retries, Monitoring, and Operational Visibility
Tasks can be configured with retries, retry delays, and failure handling. Airflow records task states and
workflow history, allowing engineers to inspect which task failed and when it failed. Logs provide
operational visibility, while dependencies ensure that downstream tasks do not continue after an
upstream failure unless the workflow explicitly allows it. This separation between orchestration and
transformation logic keeps data workflows easier to maintain.

Airflow in Data Engineering
Airflow is most useful when a pipeline contains multiple independent systems or steps that must be
coordinated. For example, a workflow may ingest files, run a Spark transformation, validate row counts,
and then refresh a downstream table. Airflow does not replace the processing engines that perform
those operations; it coordinates when and in what order they run. This distinction is important when
designing modular data platforms.

title: Apache Kafka
text:
Apache Kafka

Kafka Overview
Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used to move and retain streams of records
between producers and consumers. Instead of requiring one application to call another application
directly, producers write events to Kafka topics and consumers read those events independently. This
decoupling is useful in data engineering when many downstream systems need access to the same
stream of business events.
Topics, Partitions, and Offsets
Kafka stores events inside topics. Topics are divided into partitions so data can be distributed and
processed in parallel. Within a partition, each record receives an offset that identifies its position in the
ordered log. Consumers track offsets to know which records have already been processed. Partitioning
improves scalability, but the chosen partition key also influences ordering because Kafka guarantees
ordering within a partition rather than across an entire topic.
Producers and Consumers
A producer publishes events to a topic, while a consumer reads events from one or more topic
partitions. Consumer groups allow multiple consumers to share the work for a topic. Each partition is
assigned to only one consumer within a consumer group at a time, which allows parallel processing
while avoiding duplicate work inside that group. Different consumer groups can independently read the
same events for different use cases.
Streaming Pipelines and Delivery Semantics

consume events, transform them, and write results to a database,

Streaming Pipelines and Delivery Semantics
Kafka is often used as the transport layer for near-real-time pipelines. A downstream application may
consume events, transform them, and write results to a database, data lake, or another topic. Reliable
pipeline design requires careful handling of failures, retries, and offsets. At-least-once processing can
cause a record to be handled more than once, so downstream operations should be idempotent when
duplicates would be harmful.

Retention and Replay
Kafka retains events for a configured period rather than deleting them immediately after consumption.
This makes replay possible. A consumer can reset its offset and process older events again, which is
useful for rebuilding derived data or recovering from a bug. Replay is powerful, but the downstream
pipeline must be designed to handle repeated historical events safely and consistently.

title: Data Lakehouse Architecture
text:
Data Lakehouse Architecture

Lakehouse Overview
A data lakehouse combines the flexible storage characteristics of a data lake with management features
commonly associated with data warehouses. Data can remain in scalable object storage while table
formats and processing engines provide schema management, transactional updates, and reliable
querying. The goal is to reduce unnecessary movement between separate lake and warehouse
systems while supporting analytics and data engineering workloads on shared data.
Bronze, Silver, and Gold Layers
A common lakehouse design organizes data into Bronze, Silver, and Gold layers. Bronze contains raw
or minimally processed source data. Silver contains cleaned, standardized, and deduplicated data that
can be reused across workloads. Gold contains business-oriented tables or aggregates designed for
reporting and analytics. These layers make data quality and transformation boundaries explicit without
requiring every project to adopt exactly the same physical folder structure.
Reliable Table Management
Lakehouse table formats can add transactional behavior and metadata management on top of files
stored in object storage. This improves reliability when pipelines perform inserts, updates, or
incremental processing. Schema enforcement and schema evolution help control how table structures
change over time. Versioned table history can also support debugging, auditing, and recovery when a
pipeline writes incorrect data.

Incremental Processing
Large lakehouse pipelines should avoid repeatedly processing all historical data when only a small
amount has changed. Incremental strategies may use timestamps, watermarks, change data capture,
or source-specific identifiers to select new records. The transformation layer then merges or appends
only the required data. This reduces compute usage and shortens processing time while still keeping
curated tables current.

Serving Analytics
Gold-layer tables are commonly designed for downstream analytics. They may contain fact tables,
dimensions, aggregates, or other business-ready structures. Data engineers should preserve lineage
from raw inputs through transformations so users can understand where metrics originated. A
lakehouse architecture is strongest when storage, processing, quality checks, and governance are
treated as connected parts of the same data lifecycle.
